## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

raw_comment:
I notice that in this graph it is showing us a weekly food plan for a family of 4. I also notice that the lowest being bought and eaten in this food plan is the section called "other". Which includes soda, candy, coffee, etc. I also notice that it is expected for the families to use the most money on things that are healthy for them, such as protein and vegetables. This is probably because protein and vegetables give health benefits, when the "other" section gives much of the opposite.

I wonder why the money set aside for dairy is less than most of the other sections. I would think that people would have to spend a lot of money on items like milk, and other things that give your body dairy. I suppose this is because your body needs less dairy than protein and vegetables, or maybe dairy products just cost less. 

This relates to me and my community because it could help people buy what they actually need for their bodies at the grocery store. A lot of people end up buying just a bunch of protein, and barely any other type of food like grains and vegetables, therefore not giving their body what they need. It could also show people how they can make their body healthier, by spending a lot less money on things that they need a lot less, like soda, candy, coffee and tea.

- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.

|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

|---|---|---|

| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

The last thing I wonder is that if they were to purchase more processed foods if the weekly budget would increase or decrease.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

This graph from the Department of Agriculture sets out a suggested distribution of a staple budget. They attempt to include a 'balanced' food model for an average family of 4 people for a total of $193 per week. At first sight, it seems like a massive help for many families who benefit from this resource.

On the other hand, They suggest a diet based on animal protein, which is the highest budget, $47, regardless of how harmful the number of antibiotics, hormones, and steroids added can be for daily consumption.

Nevertheless, many scientific studies have shown that the daily consumption of animal meats is directly related to cancerous diseases. Still, unfortunately, some government institutions & health organizations continue to refer people to these types of diets.

After analyzing the "Thrifty Food Plan," there is a question: is the government interested in the people's health, or is it simply looking to benefit private companies and fulfill just one more item on its agenda?

I am convinced that the government should have an essential role in educating citizens. Therefore, it is not enough to give them the money. They have to provide them the tools to make informed decisions that impact their well-being and their families. Otherwise, it would be hard to decrease the number of heart disease deaths, overweight, and diabetes.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

1. I noticed when looking in this graph that there was a wheel of food groups with suggested options and prices for specific items related to these groups. For example, Seafood was listed under Protein. The wheel adds up the total cost of what all of these foods would be for a 4 person family and comes to the conclusion that families would only have to spend near $193 per week for food. I also noticed that the healthier foods were more expensive. I know that this is generally the case everywhere because natural ingredients are not produced as quickly as artificial foods or foods that do not require growing. 
2. I wonder what the quality of all of the foods would be with such low prices. I also wonder if this will be enough food or if everyone will have small portions and receive the bare minimum. 3. I relate to this because I know how expensive foods can be and I know that people's health can be put at risk in order to survive.

The first thing I noticed was the color coordination. When I was younger and in elementary school, they used to called a balanced diet a "rainbow." Meaning that you should have different types/colors of food on your plate at every meal. One thing that sticks out to me is how expensive everything is on this wheel. If you're someone working a low income or minimum wage job and are providing for your family, this seems like an impossible task. I also wonder how families who may have certain food allergies might adapt to this as well. I'm also wondering the quality of food that is listed at these prices, especially with the meat! I would imagine that it would be one of if not the highest expense. 

In my community, lack of food was never a problem which I'm incredibly thankful for. But I do know that there are several food banks in my area for those who don't have the privilege of going home with food on the table. Many have to make sacrifices, whether it is a balanced diet or cutting down on other necessities in order to properly nourish themselves.

## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

I notice that the allotted food budget for a family of four is $193 for one week, which would be $6.89 for one person each day. I notice that protein and vegetables have the highest allotment of money. The other category, which includes coffee and tea, has the least money. The sub-categories that have the most money are whole fruits, whole grain products, poultry, and low fat dairy products. The sub categories that have the least money are grain cereals and snacks, coffee and tea, cheese, and eggs. I notice that “red and orange” vegetables and “dark green” vegetables are separate categories.

I wonder why dairy is included in the graph even though it is not necessary for a nutritionally complete diet. I wonder why the vegetables are separated into different categories by color. I wonder why coffee and tea only get $2 when they are staple parts of the American diet. I wonder why whole fruit gets the most allotted money. I wonder why the graph specifies things like whole grain versus refined grain and low fat versus high fat.

This impacts my community because if 1 in 8 Americans receive SNAP aid, then there are people in my community who receive it. Also, any person may need advice for how much money to spend on what food.

“The Thrifty Food Plan: Eating With Less Than $7 Per Person Per Day”

Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the Department of Agriculture’s newly revised Thrifty Food Plan, the food groups used to estimate the cost of an economical, nutritious diet.   This plan is the basis of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).   Note the allocation to food groups is the basis of calculating the SNAP benefits.  Recipients can spend their benefits as they choose.  Although the payments may seem modest for middle-income Americans, the program reduces hunger, improves nutrition and lead to better health.

raw_comment: When looking at this graph, "Thrifty Food Plan," many things stick out to me. I notice that the biggest amount of spending goes towards protein and vegetables, paying $47 for protein and $46 for vegetables. This seems very reasonable because those two food categories should be focused on the most when it comes to shopping. The other biggest spending categories are dairy, grains, and fruit. These are also very reasonable spending amounts because each one is a staple to a healthy diet. I wonder why they only leave $2 for tea and coffee when it would be very hard to buy those items for that price. I also wonder how achievable spending $193 a week for a family of four is. image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |
raw_comment: Examining this "Thrifty Food Plan," I noticed how the majority of money spent on groceries focuses on protein and vegetables. There is only one dollar difference between the two food categories since they are the most important categories for the health and growth of all family members. I realized that people using food stamps still need access to different options of specific foods due to allergies, health issues, or preferences in general. The cost of each category is split up even further with the price of each section as well. This graph relates to my community because a multitude of people around me, especially in my hometown, use food stamps to buy their groceries. A headline that captures what this graph is representing is "Cost-efficient Weekly Food Plan Method For Families."

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

Honestly, I think $193 seems like a lot of money to spend on food for one week--if a person has access to an actual grocery store.
